claims.claim: Flight deficits were observed upon expression of IP3RDN during pupal development and not when expressed in adults
claims.source: Flight deficits were observed upon expression of IP3RDN during pupal development and not when expressed in adults. In pupae the deficit was most prominent by expression of the ItprDN during the shorter window of 48–96 hr APF (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal expression experiment data shown in Figure 3A

claims.claim: Flight in itprku mutant animals was rescued to a significant extent by Itpr+ expression from 48 to 96 hr APF but not when expressed before and after
claims.source: Flight in itprku mutant animals was rescued to a significant extent by Itpr+ expression from 48 to 96 hr APF (277 ± 60.3 s) but not when expressed before and after.
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B

claims.claim: Post-48 hr APF is the time period during which levels of the IP3R are upregulated in the pupal brain
claims.source: Interestingly, post-48 hr APF is also the time period during which levels of the IP3R are upregulated in the pupal brain (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data from pupal brain lysates shown in Figure 3C

claims.claim: The number of PPL1 DANs was no different between controls and in flies expressing ItprDN
claims.source: The number of PPL1 DANs was no different between controls and in flies expressing ItprDN in either TH-D or MB296B marked neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claims.claim: Projections from MB296B to the γ2α′1 MB lobes appeared unchanged upon expression of ItprDN
claims.source: Moreover, projections from MB296B to the γ2α′1 MB lobes also appeared unchanged upon expression of ItprDN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claims.claim: Adult flight bouts were significantly shorter upon stage specific knock-down (48–96 hr APF) of the mAChR in TH-D' neurons
claims.source: Adult flight bouts were significantly shorter upon stage specific knock-down (48–96 hr APF) of the mAChR in TH-D' neurons with an RNAi under temporal control of the TARGET system (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal RNAi knockdown flight assay data shown in Figure 3D

claims.claim: Knockdown of mAChR in PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs manifested mild flight defects
claims.source: Further knockdown of mAChR in PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs also manifested mild flight defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown flight assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claims.claim: Loss of synaptic vesicle recycling in pupae resulted in significantly shorter flight bout durations
claims.source: Loss of synaptic vesicle recycling in pupae resulted in significantly shorter flight bout durations of 419.9 ± 50.2 s (THD') and 411.5 ± 57 s (MB296B) as compared to controls (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by Shibirets expression flight assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claims.claim: The requirement for synaptic vesicle release was restricted to 48–96 hr APF
claims.source: The requirement for synaptic vesicle release was further restricted to 48–96 hr APF consistent with the requirement of IP3R at the same time interval (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal Shibirets expression data shown in Figure 4A and comparison with Figure 3A,B

claims.claim: Flight bout durations were reduced significantly after acute inactivation (5 min) of synaptic vesicle recycling in PPL1 DANs and the pair of PPL1-γ2α′1 subset DANs in adults
claims.source: Importantly, flight bout durations were reduced significantly after acute inactivation (5 min) of synaptic vesicle recycling in PPL1 DANs (THD') and the pair of PPL1-γ2α′1 subset (MB296B) DANs in adults, supporting a requirement for neurotransmitter release from these neurons during flight (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by acute Shibirets inactivation flight assay data shown in Figure 4A

claims.claim: The food seeking index of hungry flies with IP3RDN was reduced significantly as compared to controls
claims.source: The food seeking index of hungry flies with IP3RDN was reduced significantly as compared to controls (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 2, Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by food-seeking assay data shown in Figure 4B and C

claims.claim: Knockdown of mAChR in either PPL1 (THD') or PPL1-γ2α′1 decreased the ability of starved males to find a yeast drop
claims.source: Knockdown of mAChR in either PPL1 (THD') or PPL1-γ2α′1 decreased the ability of starved males to find a yeast drop (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 3), while fed flies were similar to genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—source data 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by food-seeking assay data with mAChR knockdown shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claims.claim: Fluorescence of Syt.eGFP in the MB lobes was no different between control brains and in presence of the IP3RDN
claims.source: Fluorescence of Syt.eGFP in the MB lobes was no different between control brains and in presence of the IP3RDN (Figure 5A), suggesting that synapse numbers were unchanged by expression of IP3RDN.
claims.evidence: Supported by synaptotagmin-GFP fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 5A and inference from comparison

claims.claim: Responding brains decreased from 77% (10/13 brains) in controls to 47% (8/17 brains) upon expression of IP3RDN
claims.source: Responding brains decreased from 77% (10/13 brains) in controls to 47% (8/17 brains) upon expression of IP3RDN.
claims.evidence: Supported by GRABDA fluorescence response data

claims.claim: GRABDA fluorescence arising from dopamine release was significantly muted amongst responders expressing the IP3RDN as compared to responders from control brains
claims.source: Moreover, GRABDA fluorescence arising from dopamine release was significantly muted amongst responders expressing the IP3RDN as compared to responders from control brains (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by GRABDA fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claims.claim: Increase in GRABDA fluorescence at the synaptic terminals in the MB was faster than the carbachol-stimulated change in GCaMP fluorescence measured in the cell body
claims.source: Interestingly, increase in GRABDA fluorescence at the synaptic terminals in the MB was faster (Figure 5C) than the carbachol-stimulated change in GCaMP fluorescence measured in the cell body as measured by time taken to reach the peak response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of GRABDA and GCaMP fluorescence kinetics shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claims.claim: Neurons expressing IP3RDN and GCaMP did not evince a significant Ca2+ response either during or after red light stimulus from optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimson
claims.source: In neurons expressing IP3RDN and GCaMP optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimsom did not evince a significant Ca2+ response either during or after the red light stimulus, as compared with the control genotype expressing RFP and GCaMP (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation and GCaMP imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B

claims.claim: There was an instant decline in Arclight fluorescence in control cells, while cells with IP3RDN showed almost no change in fluorescence after KCl-mediated depolarisation
claims.source: There was an instant decline in Arclight fluorescence in control cells, while cells with IP3RDN showed almost no change in fluorescence after KCl-mediated depolarisation (Figure 6C,D, Figure 6—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by Arclight voltage sensor imaging data shown in Figure 6C,D

claims.claim: Signaling through the IP3R is required for maintaining excitability of central neuromodulatory dopaminergic neurons
claims.source: Taken together, these observations confirm that signaling through the IP3R is also required for maintaining excitability of central neuromodulatory dopaminergic neurons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from optogenetic and depolarization experiments showing reduced excitability with IP3RDN

claims.claim: The dominant negative construct (ItprDN) was designed based on previous studies in mammalian IP3Rs
claims.source: The dominant negative construct (ItprDN) was designed based on previous studies in mammalian IP3Rs (Figure 1A; Alzayady et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Alzayady et al., 2016

claims.claim: All monomers in the IP3R tetramer need to bind IP3 for channel opening
claims.source: The mammalian dominant negative IP3R1 gene was based on the finding that all monomers in the IP3R tetramer need to bind IP3 for channel opening (Alzayady et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Alzayady et al., 2016

claims.claim: Failure of a single IP3R monomer to bind IP3 renders the resultant IP3R tetramer non-functional
claims.source: Failure of a single IP3R monomer to bind IP3 renders the resultant IP3R tetramer non-functional.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge from mammalian IP3R studies

claims.claim: Drosophila IP3Rs are tetrameric
claims.source: Drosophila IP3Rs are also tetrameric suggesting that a similar strategy for generating a dominant-negative IP3R could be used for cell-specific studies of neuronal function and behaviour.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge about Drosophila IP3R structure

claims.claim: Hypomorphic and heteroallelic combinations of Drosophila IP3R mutants exhibit flight deficits ranging from mild to strong
claims.source: Several hypomorphic and heteroallelic combinations of Drosophila IP3R mutants are viable and exhibit flight deficits ranging from mild to strong, the focus of which lies in aminergic neurons (Banerjee et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2004

claims.claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in regulation of neurite growth
claims.source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002

claims.claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in synaptic plasticity
claims.source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000

claims.claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release
claims.source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gomez et al., 2020

claims.claim: Three IP3R isotypes, IP3R1, 2 and 3 are encoded by mammalian genomes
claims.source: Three IP3R isotypes, IP3R1, 2 and 3 are encoded by mammalian genomes (Furuichi, 1994; Taylor et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Furuichi, 1994; Taylor et al., 1999

claims.claim: IP3R1 is the most prevalent isoform in neurons
claims.source: Of these, IP3R1 is the most prevalent isoform in neurons and is relevant in the context of several neurodegenerative disorders (Terry et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Terry et al., 2018

claims.claim: Human mutations in IP3R1 cause Spinocerebellar ataxia 15 (SCA15), SCA29 and Gillespie syndrome
claims.source: Human mutations in IP3R1 cause Spinocerebellar ataxia 15 (SCA15), SCA29 and Gillespie syndrome (Hasan and Sharma, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hasan and Sharma, 2020

claims.claim: Disease causing IP3R1 mutations impact ER-Ca2+ release when tested in mammalian cell lines
claims.source: Disease causing IP3R1 mutations span different domains but several are clustered in the amino terminal IP3 binding region, from where they impact ER-Ca2+ release when tested in mammalian cell lines (Ando et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ando et al., 2018

claims.claim: A common feature of neurological disorders caused by IP3R1 mutations is loss of motor-coordination or ataxia
claims.source: A common feature of these neurological disorders is loss of motor-coordination or ataxia.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge about IP3R1-related neurological disorders

claims.claim: Dendritic expression of the IP3R in Purkinje neurons determines Long Term Depression (LTD)
claims.source: Dendritic expression of the IP3R in Purkinje neurons determines Long Term Depression (LTD), a form of post-synaptic plasticity (Miyata et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Miyata et al., 2000

claims.claim: A recent study in Drosophila identified the IP3R as an essential component of post-synaptic plasticity required for decoding the temporal order of a sensory cue and a reward stimulus in Mushroom Body neurons
claims.source: Interestingly, a recent study in Drosophila also identified the IP3R as an essential component of post-synaptic plasticity, required for decoding the temporal order of a sensory cue and a reward stimulus, in neurons of a higher brain centre, the Mushroom Body (Handler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Handler et al., 2019

claims.claim: A pre-synaptic role for the IP3R has been demonstrated in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction
claims.source: A pre-synaptic role for the IP3R has been demonstrated in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Shakiryanova et al., 2011), motor neurons (Klose et al., 2010) and most recently in axonal projections of Purkinje neurons (Gomez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Shakiryanova et al., 2011; Klose et al., 2010; Gomez et al., 2020

claims.claim: Knock-down of the IP3R in serotonergic neurons did not give a flight deficit
claims.source: Knock-down of the IP3R in serotonergic neurons, that form another major subset of the tested monoaminergic neurons, did not give a flight deficit (Sadaf et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sadaf et al., 2012

claims.claim: Mild flight deficits were observed upon RNAi mediated knock down of the IP3R in dopaminergic neurons when tethered flight was tested for 30 s
claims.source: Subsequent studies identified mild flight deficits upon RNAi mediated knock down of the IP3R in dopaminergic neurons (DANs) (Pathak et al., 2015) when tethered flight was tested for 30 s.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pathak et al., 2015

claims.claim: Overexpression of a wild-type cDNA construct can partially rescue flight deficits in itpr mutants when expressed in monoaminergic neurons
claims.source: From previous reports, we know that itpr mutants are flightless and their flight deficit can be rescued partially by overexpression of a wild-type cDNA construct (Itpr+; Venkatesh et al., 2001) in monoaminergic neurons (Banerjee et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Venkatesh et al., 2001; Banerjee et al., 2004

claims.claim: In non-excitable cells Ca2+ release through the IP3R regulates growth, secretion, gene expression, and mitochondrial function
claims.source: In non-excitable cells Ca2+ release through the IP3R regulates a range of cellular events including growth, secretion (Inaba et al., 2014), gene expression (Ouyang et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Cárdenas et al., 2010; Bartok et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Inaba et al., 2014; Ouyang et al., 2014; Cárdenas et al., 2010; Bartok et al., 2019

claims.claim: Ca2+ released from the IP3R is taken up by mitochondria
claims.source: Ca2+- released from the IP3R is also taken up by mitochondria (Bartok et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bartok et al., 2019

claims.claim: The residual Ca2+ release observed in the cytosol and mitochondria is attributed to the persistence of some IP3R tetramers with all four wild-type subunits
claims.source: We attribute the residual Ca2+ release observed in the cytosol and mitochondria to the persistence of some IP3R tetramers with all four wild-type subunits, encoded by the native itpr gene.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and knowledge of IP3R tetramer assembly

claims.claim: Specification of central dopaminergic neurons is complete in late larval brains
claims.source: It is known that specification of central dopaminergic neurons is complete in late larval brains (Hartenstein et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hartenstein et al., 2017

claims.claim: Neuronal expression of the mAChR during pupal development is required for adult flight
claims.source: From a previous study, it is known that neuronal expression of the mAChR during pupal development is required for adult flight (Agrawal et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Agrawal et al., 2013

claims.claim: Acetylcholine activates the mAChR on PPL1 DANs of late pupae and/or adults to stimulate Ca2+ release through the IP3R
claims.source: Taken together our data support the idea that acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, activates the mAChR on PPL1 DANs of late pupae and/or adults to stimulate Ca2+ release through the IP3R.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including mAChR knockdown and IP3RDN expression effects

claims.claim: The 48–96 hr time window of pupal development is when adult neural circuits begin to mature with the formation of synapses
claims.source: The 48–96 hr time window of pupal development is when adult neural circuits begin to mature with the formation of synapses, some of which are eliminated whilst others are strengthened (Akin et al., 2019; Consoulas et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Akin et al., 2019; Consoulas et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2016

claims.claim: Synapse strengthening occurs when pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release leads to post-synaptic excitation/inhibition
claims.source: Synapse strengthening occurs when pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release leads to post-synaptic excitation/inhibition (Andreae and Burrone, 2018; Baines, 2003; Baines et al., 2001; Pang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Andreae and Burrone, 2018; Baines, 2003; Baines et al., 2001; Pang et al., 2010

claims.claim: IP3-mediated Ca2+ release might modulate synaptic activity and lead to strengthening of synapses between THD' DANs and their post-synaptic partners during pupal development
claims.source: We hypothesized that IP3-mediated Ca2+ release might modulate synaptic activity and hence lead to strengthening of synapses between THD' DANs and their post-synaptic partners during pupal development.
claims.evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental observations and established knowledge

claims.claim: THD' marked dopaminergic neurons require both synaptic vesicle recycling and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release during late pupal development for their adult function
claims.source: These data suggest that THD' marked dopaminergic neurons require both synaptic vesicle recycling and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release during late pupal development for their adult function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from temporal Shibirets and IP3RDN expression experiments

claims.claim: Impaired synaptic vesicle release from adult PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the ability of starved flies to identify a food source rapidly
claims.source: Impaired synaptic vesicle release from adult PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs, by expression of Shibirets, also reduces the ability of starved flies to identify a food source rapidly (Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claims.claim: Cholinergic stimulation of IP3/Ca2+ in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the motivation for longer flight bouts as well as the motivation to search for food
claims.source: Thus cholinergic stimulation of IP3/Ca2+ in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the motivation for longer flight bouts as well as the motivation to search for food.
claims.evidence: Inferred from mAChR knockdown effects on both flight and food-seeking behavior

claims.claim: Expression of IP3RDN in MB296B DANs reduced the synaptic release of dopamine at the γ2α′1 lobe
claims.source: Thus, expression of IP3RDN in MB296B DANs reduced the synaptic release of dopamine at the γ2α′1 lobe.
claims.evidence: Inferred from GRABDA fluorescence measurements showing reduced dopamine release

claims.claim: There exist a greater number of mAChRs near the synapse than on the soma of MB296B DANs
claims.source: Perhaps, there exist a greater number of mAChRs near the synapse than on the soma of MB296B DANs.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on faster GRABDA response compared to somatic GCaMP response

claims.claim: mAChRs are present on the processes of Kenyon cells in the mushroom body
claims.source: For example, mAChRs are also present on the processes of Kenyon cells in the mushroom body (Bielopolski et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2020) and form a tripartite synapse with dendrites from MB output neurons (MB-ONs) and axonal processes of MB296B DANs.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bielopolski et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2020

claims.claim: The neurotransmitter acetylcholine stimulates dopamine release in adult DANs through mAChR-IP3R signaling
claims.source: Although requirement for the IP3R and the mAChR was restricted to 48–96 hr APF, these data suggest that the neurotransmitter acetylcholine stimulates dopamine release in adult DANs through mAChR-IP3R signaling.
claims.evidence: Inferred from GRABDA experiments showing carbachol-stimulated dopamine release

claims.claim: The lack of flight deficits by adult-specific expression of IP3RDN and knockdown of mAChR is probably due to perdurance of the respective proteins from late pupae through to adults
claims.source: The lack of flight deficits by adult-specific expression of IP3RDN (Figure 3A) and knockdown of mAChR (Figure 3D) is probably due to perdurance of the respective proteins from late pupae through to adults.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on temporal expression patterns and protein stability

claims.claim: Reduced strength of MB synapses by pupal expression of IP3RDN and concomitant inhibition of synaptic vesicle release during circuit maturation may contribute to adult flight deficits
claims.source: It remains possible that reduced strength of MB synapses, by pupal expression of IP3RDN and concomitant inhibition of synaptic vesicle release during circuit maturation, also contribute to adult flight deficits.
claims.evidence: Speculated as an alternative or additional mechanism

claims.claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs are likely to receive direct excitatory inputs in addition to neuromodulatory input of acetylcholine
claims.source: In addition to the neuromodulatory input of acetylcholine, the PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs are likely to receive direct excitatory inputs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from optogenetic and depolarization experiments

claims.claim: Some MB296B neurons exhibit high basal activity even in the absence of optogenetic stimulation
claims.source: In agreement with recent findings, some MB296B neurons exhibit high basal activity even in the absence of optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Siju et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Siju et al., 2020

claims.claim: Neurons with IP3RDN fail to respond to a depolarising stimulus
claims.source: These data suggest that neurons with IP3RDN fail to respond to a depolarising stimulus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from KCl depolarization and optogenetic stimulation experiments

claims.claim: A role for the PPL1 cluster of dopaminergic neurons in modulating flight and longer flight bouts has been reported earlier
claims.source: Although insect flight is an innate behaviour the persistence of flight requires motivation presumably driven by neuromodulatory mechanisms and circuits in the central brain, that need to intersect with hard-wired flight circuits in the ventral ganglion. A role for the PPL1 cluster of dopaminergic neurons in modulating flight and longer flight bouts has been reported earlier (Pathak et al., 2015; Ravi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2015; Ravi et al., 2018

claims.claim: This is the first report identifying the two PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs as required for maintenance of flight
claims.source: However, amongst the PPL1 cluster this is the first report identifying the two PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs as required for maintenance of flight.
claims.evidence: Claimed as novel finding from this study

claims.claim: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs and their downstream Mushroom body output neuron (MBON- γ2α′1) encode the state of hunger
claims.source: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs and their downstream Mushroom body output neuron (MBON- γ2α′1) also encode the state of hunger (Tsao et al., 2018), formation and consolidation of appetitive memory (Berry et al., 2018; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2018), fat storage (Al-Anzi and Zinn, 2018), and sleep (Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2018; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2018; Al-Anzi and Zinn, 2018; Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015

claims.claim: Dopamine release from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs increased in starved flies
claims.source: These studies identified the importance of modulated dopamine release as a motivational cue wherein dopamine release from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs increased in starved flies (Tsao et al., 2018) and inhibited the activity of a cholinergic output neuron from the Mushroom Body (MBON- γ2α′1; Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claims.claim: The MBON- γ2α′1 projects to PAM neurons, the fan shaped body (FSB) and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL)
claims.source: The MBON- γ2α′1 projects to another set of central DANs, the PAM neurons (Felsenberg et al., 2017), identified as flight promoting in a previous study (Manjila et al., 2019), as well as the fan shaped body (FSB) and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL; Scaplen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Felsenberg et al., 2017; Manjila et al., 2019; Scaplen et al., 2020

claims.claim: Continuous sensory inputs are essential for flight and may reach PPL1- γ2α′1/MBON - γ2α′1 synapses through cholinergic Kenyon cells
claims.source: In addition, continuous sensory inputs are essential for flight and these may reach PPL1- γ2α′1/MBON - γ2α′1 synapses through cholinergic Kenyon cells (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 and inference about circuit connectivity

claims.claim: Carbachol-stimulated Dopamine release at the MB-γ2α′1 lobe may in part be post-synaptic to acetylcholine release from the Kenyon cells
claims.source: In this context, carbachol-stimulated Dopamine release at the MB-γ2α′1 lobe may in part be post-synaptic to acetylcholine release from the Kenyon cells.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on circuit connectivity and experimental observations

claims.claim: LAL neurons signal to descending neurons that presumably connect with the flight circuit in the ventral ganglion
claims.source: Amongst these the LAL neurons signal to descending neurons (Namiki et al., 2018; Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016) that presumably connect with the flight circuit in the ventral ganglion.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Namiki et al., 2018; Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016 and inference about circuit connectivity

claims.claim: LAL neurons in locusts exhibit flight correlated activity changes
claims.source: This idea is broadly supported by the observation that LAL neurons in locusts exhibit flight correlated activity changes (Homberg, 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Homberg, 1994

claims.claim: The FSB processes visual inputs for flight navigation
claims.source: The FSB processes visual inputs for flight navigation (Weir and Dickinson, 2015) and functions during turning behaviour (Shiozaki et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Weir and Dickinson, 2015; Shiozaki et al., 2020

claims.claim: In cockroaches, activation of the FSB induces turns
claims.source: In cockroaches, activation of the FSB induces turns (Guo and Ritzmann, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Guo and Ritzmann, 2013

claims.claim: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs receive inputs for assessing the internal state through multiple GPCRs including sNPFR, Insulin receptor, AstA receptor and a serotonin receptor 5HT1B
claims.source: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs receive inputs for assessing the internal state through multiple GPCRs including certain neuropeptide receptors such as sNPFR, Insulin receptor and AstA receptor and a serotonin receptor 5HT1B (Albin et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Albin et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018

claims.claim: Each of the GPCR signals appear to integrate hunger with food seeking behaviour
claims.source: Each of these signals appear to integrate hunger with food seeking behaviour (Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claims.claim: Modulated activity in the PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs serves as a 'sensor' followed by inhibition of MBON - γ2α′1, that forms an important multisensory 'integrating component' for control of downstream 'effector' circuits
claims.source: We propose that modulated activity in the PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs serves as a 'sensor' followed by inhibition of MBON - γ2α′1, that forms an important multisensory 'integrating component' for control of downstream 'effector' circuits.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on integration of experimental findings and literature

claims.claim: Appropriate MBON- γ2α′1 outputs are required to maintain long flight bouts, similar to the maintenance of wakefulness and increase in the search for food when hungry
claims.source: Appropriate MBON- γ2α′1 outputs are required to maintain long flight bouts, similar to the maintenance of wakefulness (Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015) and increase in the search for food when hungry (Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015; Tsao et al., 2018

claims.claim: Genetic manipulations that target intracellular calcium signaling are known to affect the intrinsic excitability of neurons

claims.claim: Reduced excitability of dopaminergic neurons expressing the IP3RDN transgene supports a role for intracellular calcium signals in setting the threshold of membrane excitability in response to neuromodulatory signals
claims.source: Reduced excitability of dopaminergic neurons expressing the IP3RDN transgene (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) further supports a role for intracellular calcium signals in setting the threshold of membrane excitability in response to neuromodulatory signals, such as acetylcholine (this study), the FMRFa neuropeptide (Ravi et al., 2018), and glutamate (Ryu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations

claims.claim: mAChR stimulated ER-Ca2+ signals through the IP3R regulate synaptic release of dopamine from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs during circuit maturation and during adult flight
claims.source: Because short flight bouts are also observed upon acute inhibition of vesicle recycling in adults our data support a model where mAChR stimulated ER-Ca2+ signals through the IP3R regulate synaptic release of dopamine from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs during circuit maturation and during adult flight.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on integration of experimental findings

results.result: A dominant-negative IP3R (IP3RDN) was generated by mutating three conserved residues in the Drosophila IP3R ligand binding domain. Expression of IP3RDN significantly reduced carbachol-stimulated Ca2+ responses in both cytosol and mitochondria of neurons, validating its efficacy as a tool to attenuate IP3R function.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 provide strong experimental validation of the IP3RDN construct through western blots (C3), cytosolic Ca2+ measurements (C4), and mitochondrial Ca2+ measurements (C5). The design rationale is well-supported by prior mammalian studies (C34-C36) and conservation across species (C1). The residual Ca2+ release is appropriately attributed to wild-type tetramers (C55).

results.result: IP3R function is required in a specific subset of dopaminergic neurons (PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs) for maintenance of long flight bouts. Expression of IP3RDN, IP3R RNAi, or overexpression of wild-type IP3R in these neurons all resulted in significantly shortened flight durations, with the strongest deficits observed in PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs marked by MB296BGAL4.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent genetic manipulations (IP3RDN, RNAi, overexpression) converge on the same phenotype (C6-C9), providing strong evidence. The progressive narrowing from pan-neuronal to specific dopaminergic subsets (C7, C13-C14) is methodologically sound. Rescue experiments in mutants (C10-C12) further validate the requirement. This represents a novel identification of PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs (C75).

results.result: IP3R and mAChR function are required during a critical developmental window (48-96 hr APF) in dopaminergic neurons for adult flight behavior. This temporal requirement coincides with IP3R upregulation in pupal brains and does not affect neuronal number or gross morphology, suggesting a role in circuit maturation rather than neuronal specification.
results.evaluation: Temporal expression experiments using GAL80ts clearly define the 48-96 hr APF window (C15-C16, C20-C21). This is corroborated by IP3R protein upregulation during this period (C17). The lack of effects on cell number and projections (C18-C19) rules out developmental specification defects. The convergence of IP3R and mAChR requirements (C20-C21, C57-C58) supports a signaling pathway model.

results.result: Synaptic vesicle recycling in PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs is required both during the 48-96 hr APF developmental window and acutely in adults for flight maintenance. This requirement parallels the temporal requirement for IP3R function, suggesting that IP3R-mediated Ca2+ signals regulate dopamine release during both circuit maturation and adult function.
results.evaluation: Shibirets experiments demonstrate requirements during both pupal development (C22-C23) and acute adult function (C24), paralleling IP3R requirements. The temporal overlap with IP3R function (C23, C62) supports a mechanistic link. The model is consistent with prior literature on ER-Ca2+ regulation of vesicle release (C97-C98).

results.result: IP3R and mAChR function in PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs is required for food-seeking behavior in starved flies. Expression of IP3RDN or knockdown of mAChR significantly reduced the ability of hungry flies to locate food, suggesting these neurons integrate internal state with motivated behaviors.
results.evaluation: Food-seeking assays show consistent deficits with both IP3RDN expression (C25) and mAChR knockdown (C26) in the same neuronal populations. The specificity to starved flies and consistency with prior Shibirets studies (C63) strengthen the conclusion. This links the same neurons to multiple motivated behaviors (C64).

results.result: Expression of IP3RDN in PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs reduces carbachol-stimulated dopamine release at mushroom body synapses without affecting synapse number. The proportion of responding brains decreased from 77% to 47%, and responders showed significantly attenuated GRABDA fluorescence, indicating that IP3R-mediated Ca2+ signals regulate dopamine release.
results.evaluation: Synaptotagmin-GFP measurements rule out changes in synapse number (C27), isolating the effect to synaptic function. GRABDA measurements provide direct evidence of reduced dopamine release (C28-C29, C65). The faster kinetics at terminals versus soma (C30) suggests local regulation. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (C68) supports the mechanistic model.

results.result: IP3R-mediated Ca2+ signaling is required for maintaining neuronal excitability in PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs. Neurons expressing IP3RDN failed to respond to optogenetic stimulation or KCl-mediated depolarization, as measured by GCaMP and Arclight voltage sensors, suggesting IP3R regulates membrane excitability through modulation of ion channel function.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches (optogenetics C31, KCl depolarization C32, voltage imaging C32) converge on reduced excitability (C33, C73). The findings are consistent with prior studies in other systems (C89-C91) and supported by known mechanisms of Ca2+-dependent ion channel regulation (C92-C95). The basal activity observation (C72) provides additional context.

results.result: The 48-96 hr APF window represents a critical period for synapse maturation when IP3-mediated Ca2+ release may modulate synaptic activity to strengthen connections between dopaminergic neurons and their postsynaptic partners. The lack of adult-specific effects may reflect protein perdurance from pupal stages.
results.evaluation: While the temporal window is well-established (C59) and synapse strengthening mechanisms are supported by literature (C60), the specific hypothesis about IP3R function in synapse strengthening (C61) remains speculative. The perdurance explanation (C69) and alternative synapse strength hypothesis (C70) are reasonable but unproven. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between developmental and acute requirements.

results.result: PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs and their downstream MBON-γ2α'1 form part of a circuit that integrates internal state (hunger) and sensory inputs to control motivated behaviors including flight and food-seeking. The authors propose a model where PPL1-γ2α'1 DANs serve as sensors, MBON-γ2α'1 as integrators, and downstream circuits (PAM, LAL, FSB) as effectors.
results.evaluation: The circuit model is well-supported by extensive prior literature on these neurons' roles in hunger (C76-C77), memory (C76), and connectivity (C78-C84). The integration of multiple GPCR inputs (C85-C86) supports the sensor function. However, the specific sensor-integrator-effector model (C87-C88) is largely inferential, synthesizing current findings with prior work. The model is plausible but requires further direct testing.

results.result: Prior work establishes that IP3Rs play diverse roles in neuronal function including neurite growth, synaptic plasticity, and neurotransmitter release in both vertebrates and Drosophila. IP3R mutations cause human ataxias, and Drosophila IP3R mutants exhibit flight deficits that can be partially rescued by expression in monoaminergic neurons.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations (C38-C54, C56-C57). They provide essential context for the current study. Claim C66 is speculative about mAChR distribution but is clearly marked as such. Claim C67 is well-supported by citations.
